A supercell spawned a brief tornado touchdown which destroyed small outbuildings, tore the roof of a garage off and slammed it into the west side of the house, broke a skylight on the house, and damaged the roof of the house.  Baseball size hail accompanying the tornado tore holes in the metal siding on the house.  This same supercell produced 3 other brief tornadoes in Chase County.

A supercell tornado touched down and overturned 3 pivot irrigation systems, broke off trees and 3 power poles as it moved northeast for less than a mile.  The supercell also produced 3 other tornadoes in Chase County.

A supercell storm that produced several tornadoes also produced up to tennis ball size hail from Champion to approximately 3 miles south of Champion.  The hail broke out hundreds of windows in homes and vehicles, tore holes in metal siding on homes, severely damaged roofs on buildings and vehicle bodies, and destroyed wheat and corn crops.
A supercell storm that produced several tornadoes south and west of Champion also produced large hail at Imperial.  The hail damaged several roofs of homes and numerous vehicle bodies.

Very heavy rain from thunderstorms produced flash flooding across much of southwest Chase County.  Two to three inches of rain fell in less than an hour causing flooding of streets in Imperial and Champion and lowland flooding along Highway 61 near Imperial.

A fire developed approximately 5 miles northeast of Wellfleet at approximately 7:30 PM CDT on March 15th. Aided by very low relative humidity and gusty winds, the fire spread to approximately 900+ acres before it was contained on March 20th. Resources from 25 local fire departments, along with personnel from the Nebraska National Guard, provided ground and aerial support for the fire. The fire was in very hilly, canyon type terrain, and was fueled by stands of cedar trees. This made attacking the fire difficult. By the 20th, improving weather conditions, allowed the fire to be contained. The main damage was to fencing as no structures were reported damaged.

All but the southwest corner of Blaine County was designated as D2 (severe drought) through the month of July.
Far eastern Boyd County remained in D3 (extreme drought), while central portions of the county remained in D2 (severe drought) throughout July. The far western section was designated as D1.
Virtually all of Brown County (except along the Niobrara River) was designated as D2 (severe drought) throughout July.
Extreme drought (D3) was expanded to cover all of Chase County during the July 12 update of the drought monitor, where the southwest corner was previously designated as D2.
Severe drought (D2) remained for western and southern portions of Custer County throughout July, while D2 was upgraded to D1 in the northeast during the July 12 update.
Extreme drought (D3) was expanded to include central and eastern Deuel County during the July 26 update. Previously, the entire county was designated as at least D2.

Severe drought (D2) was expanded northward to Valentine, the Niobrara Valley, and essentially the eastern half of the county during the July 19 drought monitor update. Previously, northeast Cherry County was designated as D1.
Western Frontier County remained in extreme drought (D3), while central and northeast portions remained in severe drought (D2) throughout the month. Southeast was designated as D1.

Southern Garden County, generally along and south of the North Platte River, remained in D2 (severe drought) throughout the month. Extreme drought (D3) clips the far southeast during the July 26 update. Otherwise, the central and northern portions were classified as D0 and D1.
All but the southeast corner of Garfield County started the month in severe drought (D2). The July 12 update removed virtually all of D2 from the county, replacing with D1.
All of Hayes County remained in extreme drought (D3) throughout July.

Eastern Holt County remained in D3 (extreme drought) throughout the month, except for a localized improvement to D2 near O'Neill during the July 19 update. The remainder of the county was classified as D2 (severe drought) for all of July.
The northeast portions of Hooker County remained in D2 (severe drought) throughout the month. The southwest corner was designated as D0, while the central portions continued as D1.

All but the northern edges of Keith County were classified as D3 (extreme drought) by the end of the month. The northern half of the county began July as D1 and southern half as D2 (severe drought), but successive downgrades were issued July 19 and 26.

All but the northwest section of Lincoln County started July as D2 (severe drought). Successive downgrades for July 19 and 26 resulted in the southwest being classified as D3 (extreme drought) and the remainder as D2.
The southern half of Logan County remained in D2 (severe drought) through the month of July, with a slight expansion on July 19. The northern portions were classified as D1.

The highest wind gust recorded was at the nearby Pine Ridge ASOS, with a peak gust of 69 mph at 1152 am MST. Sustained winds of 40 mph with gusts over 60 mph at times occurred across northern Sheridan County during the late morning through the early afternoon hours.

A fire initiated along a trail during the mid afternoon hours of October 2nd in north central portions of the Nebraska National Forest at Halsey. Aided by very strong southerly winds, the fire quickly spread to the north and north northwest consuming the Nebraska 4 H camp. At this camp, 18 buildings were destroyed including the main lodge. The fire then jumped the Middle Loup River and Nebraska highway 2 racing across several miles of open rangeland. One firefighter perished from a medical emergency while battling the fire. Approximately 200-250 different personnel battled this fire from the 2nd through the 11th. When the fire was fully extinguished, 19000 total acres had burned.

Fire started in the McCann Canyon area approximately 10 miles south of Kilgore. Known as the McCann fire and aided by strong southerly winds, the fire raced 8 miles to the north approaching the town of Kilgore late Tuesday April 11th. The town of Kilgore was evacuated as a precaution and fire crews were able to keep the fire from reaching it. Approximately 7000 acres of mainly grassland were consumed in the fire. No injuries or deaths were reported.

Fire started approximately 15 miles north of Burwell during the morning of April 11th. Named the Lowry Fire and aided by strong southerly winds, low relative humidity, and hot temperatures, the fire traveled north approximately 6 miles to the north northeast consuming approximately 6000 acres. Along with two injuries, a total of four structures were destroyed including a storage building at the Rowse Hydraulic Rake Factory. The fire was contained on April 13th.

Fire initiated along highway 2 in the vicinity of the Cooksley Ranch, 6 miles northwest of Anselmo during the morning hours of April 12th. Known as the Cooksley Complex Fire, strong southerly winds pushed the fire to the north and north northwest during the afternoon hours of the 12th. Dry lightning and a wind shift forced the fire east on the 13th. By the time the fire was contained on the morning of April 14th, it had consumed approximately 37000 acres of rangeland. A home was destroyed at the McGinn Ranch and a bunkhouse was lost as well. Several calves were also lost in the fire in addition to outbuildings.

A grass fire developed on the southeast side of the Hillcrest Addition north of North Platte. Aided by strong northwesterly winds behind an exiting cold front, fire raced approximately 4 miles to the south southeast before ending along and north of Hall School Road. No buildings were consumed in the fire, however 1000 acres of grassland was burned.

A fire developed 7 miles west of Stapleton during the late afternoon hours of February 26. Aided by strong westerly winds, the fire raced east, barely missing the town of Stapleton. The town was evacuated as a precaution, but the fire missed the town. Approximately 7000 acres of rangeland was burned in the fire. The fire was under control by mid evening.

A fire started along Betty Way Road north of North Platte at approximately 1030 AM CT on February 26th. Aided by 40+ MPH westerly winds, the fire raced 26 miles east into western portions of Custer County. By the time the fire was completely contained on September 29th, over 71000 acres of rangeland had burned. A farmstead north of Maxwell was completely destroyed by the fire. In addition the farmstead, approximately a half a dozen outbuildings were destroyed along with numerous wind breaks and fencing.

The tornado continued east, damaging outbuildings and overturning a third pivot.  The tornado traveled further east, overturning a semi trailer, damaging a shelter belt and striping shingles and siding off a house at a farmstead. The tornado then tracked northeast, where it flipped a fourth center pivot, and damaged outbuildings at a farmstead. The tornado traveled another mile to the northeast before dissipating. Before it dissipated two more center pivot irrigation systems were destroyed.

A wildfire broke out at around 1 PM CDT on October 7th in the vicinity of Old highway 83 and Zlomke road south-southeast of North Platte. Aided by southerly winds, the fire tracked quickly to the north-northeast it burned approximately 725 acres of mixed grass and cedar trees. Five homesteads were evacuated along State Farm Road between Newberry Access and Shack Road. A total of 13 fire departments aided in the fire and aerial support was brought in to aid in fire suppression. Evacuation orders were lifted by mid afternoon and the fire was contained around 6 PM CDT.  No structures were damaged in the fire and the fire was confined to pasture and canyon ground.

Fire initiated during the afternoon hours of December 19th near Round Valley Road and 803 Drive, approximately 3 miles northeast of the Broken Bow Municipal Airport. Aided by strong northwesterly winds, the fire raced southeast, consuming approximately 2800 acres of mainly grassland and 3 unoccupied structures. The fire was brought under control on December 21st, then re-ignited on December 22nd.  The fire was finally brought under control by December 23rd. One indirect fatality was reported as a result of the fire. A person operating a UTV, in the process of moving cattle away from the fire, was ejected as a result of an accident and died from his injuries.

A supercell tornado touched down just north-northeast of Rose in Rock County and entered Holt County approximately 13 miles south-southwest of Stuart and continued for another 10 miles before dissipating 3 miles south-southeast of Stuart.  In Holt County, the multiple vortex tornado broke off power poles, destroyed outbuildings, overturned several center pivot irrigation systems, snapped and uprooted numerous large trees, damaged roofs, and moved vehicles.  The tornado maintained the EF2 rating in both Rock and Holt Counties.  The average path width in Holt County was 30 yards with the maximum width of 50 yards.

This multiple vortex tornado formed near Rose and tracked northeast for about 20 miles before exiting Rock County about 13 miles south-southeast of Newport at 1500 CST.  In Rock County, the tornado broke power poles, shifted a house off its foundation a few inches, destroyed outbuildings, overturned a couple of center pivot irrigation systems, and snapped trees.  The tornado maintained the EF2 intensity through Rock and Holt County.  The average path width in Rock County was 30 yards.

Heavy rain from thunderstorms caused flash flooding along Ponca Creek in Boyd County.  Up to 4 inches of rain fell with approximately 3 inches of it falling in 30 minutes.  The water runoff washed over roadways near Spencer and inundated the commercial area of Bristow.  Several secondary roads were completely or partially washed away.
The strong thunderstorm winds ripped off shingles from a home and broke off large tree limbs.

The fire then flared up and was renamed the East Table Fire. Two firefighters were injured on February 24th when their fire truck overturned in hilly terrain. The East Table Fire consumed an additional 450 acres before it was contained on March 3rd.  A third fire was reported over western portions of Custer County. Named the Eureka Valley Fire, this fire consumed approximately 4800 acres and burned from February 24th through March 3rd when it was finally 100 percent contained.

Fire initiated during the early afternoon hours of April 21st. Aided by gusty southerly winds, the fire tracked north consuming approximately 24000 acres of grass and timberland. The fire tracked through several canyons, making control of the fire difficult. By the time the fire was contained, around 50 agencies assisted with the fire, including numerous local fire departments, US Forest Service, Bureau of Indian Affairs, NEMA, State Fire Marshal, Nebraska National Guard, Nebraska State Patrol, Nebraska Game and Parks and Nebraska Forest Service responded to the fire. One cabin was consumed in the fire along with 8 utility poles and around 60 head of cattle lost and 20 cattle burnt in the blaze.

Fire started at the Otter Creek Ranch north northwest of highway 92 on the west end of Lake McConaughy. With gusty northwesterly winds, the fire tracked to the southeast leading to the evacuation of houses north of highway 92 in the Cedar View development. Firefighters were able to contain the fire before it reached those homes and the evacuation was lifted mid afternoon. A total of 1000 to 1200 acres of grassland was consumed by the fire. A total of 11 different fire departments battled the blaze.

Fire initiated during the early afternoon hours of March 12th east of Angora in Morrill County. Aided by 50 MPH west-northwest winds, the fire entered Garden County. By the time the fire was contained on March 28th, approximately 496,565 acres of rangeland was consumed in the fire. A total of 10 outbuildings and 1 primary residence was destroyed. Livestock losses were estimated at 200 sheep, 10 calves and 200 cattle lost in Garden County.

Fire initiated during the early afternoon hours of March 12th east of Angora in Morrill County. Aided by 50 MPH winds, the fire tracked east of Garden County and spread across southwestern Arthur County. By the time the fire was contained on March 28th, approximately 64,590 acres of rangeland was consumed in the fire. The fire resulted in one fatality in southwestern Arthur County. One primary residence was destroyed, along with 6 outbuildings damaged in the fire. Two calf-cow pairs were lost in the fire in Arthur County.

The Morrill fire entered northwestern Keith County during the evening hours of March 12th prompting the evacuation of residences and approximately 300 persons on the northwest side of Lake McConaughy. The fire continued and was contained on March 28th. A total of 37,212 acres were consumed in the fire and one outbuilding was destroyed.
The Morrill fire entered southwestern Grant County during the evening hours of March 12th. The fire consumed 872 acres of rangeland in Grant County.

Fire initiated during the late afternoon hours of March 12th. Aided by strong west-northwest winds, the fire pushed quickly to the southeast. By the time the fire was contained on March 27th, a total of 106,194 acres was consumed in Lincoln County. The fire led to approximately, 300 persons being evacuated around Jeffrey Lake on March 12th. One injury occurred as a result of the fire. Three fire vehicles were destroyed in the fire.

Fire started approximately 9 miles south of Kilgore during the afternoon hours of March12th. West winds initially pushed the fire east. By evening, a cold front shifted the winds to the north, forcing the fire south. By the time the fire was totally contained on the 23rd, a total of 17,229 acres of rangeland was consumed. One primary residence was consumed in the fire, along with one cabin and three outbuildings. Approximately 10 head of livestock were lost in the fire.

Fire initiated during the mid afternoon hours approximately 8 miles west-southwest of Halsey. Aided by strong west, then north winds, the fire moved east then south across a large portion of the Nebraska National Forest. By the time the fire was contained, 27,292 acres were consumed.

Fire initiated shortly after midnight MDT of March 26th approximately 2 miles north of Ashby. Aided by strong northerly winds, the fire raced to the south consuming approximately 34,748 acres in Grant County. Ashby and Hyannis were evacuated the night of the 26th. Four primary structures were consumed in the fire along with fencing and 3 outbuildings.
The Ashby fire spread across western portions of Grant County, ending up in portions of northeastern Garden County. A total of 1,259 acres of rangeland was consumed in the fire.

Lightning started a fire north of Mullen in southern Cherry County during the late evening hours of April 20th. Named the Spike Box fire, and aided by strong winds, the fire grew to approximately 7,000 acres before rainfall helped extinguish the fire on April 22nd. One grass rig was damaged in the fire. A total of 8 fire departments responded to the blaze. A total of 3 residences had to be evacuated at the Spike Box Ranch headquarters. No structures were lost in the fire.

These dangerous wind chill values persisted for nearly 8 hours, through the late morning hours on January 7th, as winds continued to diminish.

Winter storm conditions occurred across Boyd County during the afternoon and evening hours on January 6th, 2010, as strong northwest winds of 30 to 40 mph and gusty combined with falling snow.  Snow accumulations of 3 to 5 inches were reported.  Visibilities were reduced as low as a quarter mile at times and many primary and secondary roads were closed by late afternoon and early evening.  Although the snow ended by early evening, strong northwest winds persisted overnight to cause continued blowing and drifting snow and reduced visibility. Some power outages were also reported.

At 845 PM CDT, the tornado touched down over an open field west of Sparks and traveled east where it struck a metal building tearing off the southwest facing roof. At 930 PM CDT, a tornado touched down approximately 12 miles northwest of Springview and traveled northeast for 20 minutes before lifting 11 miles north of Springview. The tornado did extensive tree damage when it touched down, then moved northeast and struck two farmsteads. At the first farmstead, a loafing shed and stock trailer were destroyed, extensive tree and fence damage occurred, and a roof was torn off an old hog building. The most extensive damage occurred north of the farmstead where six rural electric association poles where broken.  The tornado continued to move northeast and destroy a windmill.  Then a second farmstead was hit with the tornado destroying a 40 by 60 feet quonset building before the tornado lifted at 950 PM CDT.

Ericson Dam in Wheeler County, Nebraska failed Sunday evening, June 13th. Heavy rainfall contributed to water levels at the Ericson Dam that exceeded the maximum dam height, and water flowed into the emergency spillway. As debris gathered the spillway began to erode before 7 p.m. CST and the spillway breached, thereafter causing water to drain from the lake. Water levels behind the dam were estimated at 23 or 24 feet prior to dam failure. The floodwater flowed down Cedar River where the floodwater impacted approximately 15 homes and farmland in Wheeler County. At 845 p.m. CST, the floodwater reached the Wheeler and Greeley County line, with 6 inches of water was flowing over the Highway 281 bridge.

A garage was leveled with the roof blown 100 yards to the north. The garage siding was wrapped around trees. The rest of the building was laying on the ground in a pile.

A storm hit Ainsworth with damage significant that included the destruction of two buildings and many trees. Power lines were also downed by the winds and resulted in a power outage that lasted about two hours. The damage was most severe in a relatively concentrated zone, on the north side of the town, which is consistent with a microburst damage path. It was in that area where one of the buildings was destroyed. Debris from the steel building was scattered to the north up to 200 yards, and steel was twisted violently around trees north of the building site.
The public reported winds downed tree branches at least 4 inches in diameter.
Winds destroyed a 90 by 30 building.

The strong winds destroyed a 20 X 30 open faced garage and 8 X 10 garden shed 3 miles south of Broken Bow on highway 21.
The strong winds were accompanied by quarter size hail.

A 40 X 60 Wick steel storage building was damaged when lifted by strong winds. The building had several trusses splintered and shifted before approximately 20 feet of the peak panels broke with the structure slammed back to the foundation. A 26 foot horse trailer was also moved two to three feet. In addition, southwest of Broken Bow a lean-to congregated steel roof on a large barn was damaged as the winds lifted and peeled panels off. A center irrigation pivot was also overturned.

Heavy rainfall led to the failure of a 50 foot dam near 3 miles southwest of Broken Bow on highway 21. The flood water moved down toward the southwest edge of town to impact the Callaway road one mile west of town and highway 21 as water flowed across the roads. Rainfall gage estimates around town measured up to 4.5 inches with several streets and homes in town flooded as well due to heavy rain.

A fire began in Lincoln County when a combine ignited the fire while harvesting soybeans. A Red Flag Warning was in effect where strong winds helped spread the fire quickly and burning an estimated 40 square miles of acres that encompassed corn and soybean crops. A home and barn, along with a number of farm machinery damaged or destroyed as the fire spread from northern Lincoln County into Logan County to near the town of Stapleton. As the fire approached the city emergency crews closed Highway 83 and a mandatory evacuation of the community. One landowner was hospitalized due to inhalation as fire crews worked through the night to control hot spots.

This tornado formed 21 miles north northeast of North Platte in rural Lincoln County. The tornado tracked northeast for less than a mile before exiting Lincoln County about 21.82 miles northeast of North Platte at 1635 CST. The tornado continued in Logan County another 5 miles before dissipating at 1639 CST. In Lincoln County the tornado moved across open rangeland where no damage was observed. While in Lincoln and Logan counties the tornado was rated an EF0. The average path width in Lincoln County was 20 yards.

This tornado formed 21 miles north northeast of North Platte in Lincoln County and entered Logan County about 6 miles southwest of Stapleton at 1635 CST. The tornado then continued for another 2 miles, briefly lifting after moving across the county line, and dissipating 4 miles southwest of Stapleton at 1639 CST.  In Logan County scattered tree damage occurred to include damage to a tree wind break line and a center pivot irrigation system sustained damaged to three sections before the tornado dissipating. While in Lincoln and Logan counties the tornado was rated an EF0. Average path width in Logan County was 20 yards.
Doors blown off of machine shed.
Half inch size hail covered the ground.

A tornado touched down 10 miles southwest of North Platte and traveled north and destroyed a large metal transmission tower.  Two homes were damaged, several outbuildings and garages were damaged or destroyed.  Two center pivot irrigation systems were overturned with one wood transmission tower destroyed and extensive power line damage along the path in addition to tree damage.  The tornado dissipated while moving north of Walker road.

A tornado touched down 5 miles west southwest of North Platte just south of Interstate 80.  The tornado moved north where a semi tractor and trailer was destroyed and driver injured.  Extensive debris spread north and northwest as the tornado tracked northwest damaging a garage, overturning a center pivot irrigation system, destroying fence line and producing extensive tree damage along a one and a half mile long path before lifting just south of the South Platte river.

A tornado touched down four and a half miles west of North Platte just south of west Front street and traveled north northeast.  The tornado damage was extensive to include two homes destroyed and two additional homes with significant damage from trees blown over and windows blown out.  Two residents were injured in their homes.  As the tornado traveled north across the Union Pacific Bailey Yards, an estimated 15 tanker cars were blown over and debris was scattered northeast for one and a half miles.  A center pivot irrigation system was overturned north of Highway 30 before the tornado lifted five and a half miles northwest of North Platte.

A tornado touched down five miles west northwest of North Platte, just south of Platte Valley Road, where a two story barn was destroyed with several outbuildings damaged.  The tornado tracked northeast where a field of boards from the barn were driven into the ground, along with other debris.  As the tornado tracked northeast, two homes were damaged, a garage had structural damage, and an outbuilding was destroyed.  Extensive tree damage occurred before the tornado dissipated five miles northwest of North Platte.

A tornado touched down approximately five miles south southeast of Ringgold in McPherson County and tracked north and northwest before dissipating near the Ringgold church.  Tornado damage included several large tree limbs broken off, cedar trees uprooted, a center pivot irrigation system twisted and overturned, damage to a church building and small storage building.  The tornado was on the ground intermittently for four minutes.
Public reported a tornado briefly touched down over open rangeland near Highway 83 north of Valentine.
Public reported a forty feet by 22 feet shed was destroyed.  This was a result of damaging outflow winds from a severe thunderstorm.

Strong downburst winds caused a semi-truck to be blown off  Interstate 80 and overturned at the Roscoe interchange near mile-marker 134 and produced one injury.

Downburst winds destroyed a two car garage, snapped a 12 inch diameter pine tree in half eight feet above the ground and downed several large cottonwood tree limbs.  In the same area, the strong winds caused two power poles to bend over at 45 degree angles.
Downburst winds blew a car off the road along Interstate Highway 80 at mile-marker 137 with one injury.
A funnel cloud was spotted looking southeast of Whitman.  The parent storm that was producing the funnel cloud was also rotating.

The combination of high stream flows due to releases from Lake McConaughy and heavy rain upstream of North Platte caused the North Platte River to rise above flood stage.  The river remained above flood stage for one day, then after thunderstorms produced another two to four inches of rain just upstream of North Platte, the river once again briefly rose above flood stage.  The river crested at 6.08 feet at 6 p.m. CDT on the 13th, with minor flooding occurring.

Heavy rain fell upstream of the river gage along the North Platte River at North Platte (NPTN1). The river had already been experiencing high flows due to releases from Kingsley Dam on Lake McConaughy, and the increased runnoff caused the river to briefly rise above flood stage. The river crested at 6.07 feet at 6 a.m. CDT on April 28th.
Heavy rain caused water to flow over State Highway 93 between Stapleton and the Logan County and McPherson County line.  The water was observed over the road approximately 11 miles west of Stapleton.

Widespread street flooding occurred across the city of North Platte between 7:00 p.m. CDT to 8:30 p.m. CDT.  At one point, the water running through the streets was more than one foot in depth, while the water was up to two feet in depth at the intersection of Buffalo Bill Avenue and 2nd Street.
The hail covered the ground.  The largest hailstones were the size of quarters.
Hail covered the ground up to three inches in depth.
Golf ball size hail fell just south of the city of North Platte, at the junction of U.S. Highway 83 and Dodge Hill Road.

Tennis ball size hail fell on the west side of North Platte, with a few pieces that large also falling on the east side of the city.  Golf ball size hail also fell across much of the city and lasted until 6:50 p.m. CDT.  In some parts of the city large hail fell off and on for almost two hours.

Baseball size hail caused extensive damage to windows and siding.
The largest hail in the area measured 1.50 inches in diameter, although most of the hail was up to quarter size.

The tornado briefly touched down just south of the Flying J Truckstop, southeast of North Platte.  No damage occurred from this tornado.
The tornado was on the ground for 23 minutes and traveled northeast for 15 miles lifting intermittently while moving across open rangeland and cropland.
The funnel cloud lowered down but never touched the ground.

A tornado briefly touched down and lifted with no damage reported.

Hail up to one inch in diameter covered the ground to three inches in depth.
A tornado was on the ground for several minutes and approached State Farm Road on the southwest side of North Platte. No damage occurred from this tornado.

A dry downburst caused wind gusts up to 78 mph for approximately 20 minutes. The strong winds toppled several large trees. As the winds descended a heat burst resulted in the temperature rising 9 degrees and the dew point dropped 11 degrees.

Severe drought conditions (D2), which began the month of June, intensified to extreme drought conditions (D3) by the end of the month.  Pastures that make up close to 92 percent of the land use in Arthur County (2007 Census USDA) was rated 69% poor or very poor. The lack of rain limited grazing capacity and created increased sales of livestock as the departure from normal precipitation reached -3.0 inches. On July 23rd all counties in Nebraska were approved for CRP Emergency Haying and Grazing. Some producers have cropped silage of their corn. The drought continued into August.

Lightning ignited a wildfire in northwest Brown County north of Johnstown, along the Fairfield Creek, a tributary of the Niobrara River. The fire's initial 7 mile wide reach was fanned by strong winds to spread the fire north and jumped the Niobrara River into southwest Keya Paha County. The wildfire was named the Fairfield Creek and later renamed the Region 24 Complex as two more fires developed in eastern Keya Paha County. The fires burned a total of 75,872 acres that destroyed rangeland and timbers within Brown County, 14 homes and 17 associated outbuilding in Keya Papa County, and additional range and crop lands in eastern Cherry County and southeast Keya Paha County. Four injuries were reported, but not life threatening. As the wildfire spread north toward Highway 12, officials closed the highway and announced volunteer evacuations for Meadville and Norden that were rescinded on the 25th. The 26th the Niobrara River was closed downstream of Smith Falls State Park. The wildfire was reported 100 percent contained on the 30th, with a cost near $8,000,000.00.

A wildfire ignited by lightning in late August continued into September to burn approximately 44,159 acres in Nebraska before being contained on September 4th. The wildfire spread north into South Dakota for a total of 77,159 acres burned before containment. Initial assessments showed the wildfire burned approximately 100 power poles. The Rushville Sheriff requested an Evacuate Immediate (NWEM) message as the fire spread into parks and to alert homeowners and campers in the area. The fire stats showed 50 to 60 outbuildings destroyed, and approximately 10 homes damaged as well as two homes and two commercial properties destroyed.  The Nebraska National Guard was deployed (14 personnel) to help fight the fire, which included the use of two type three helicopters and one Blackhawk helicopter.  Many roads in the area were closed as the fire burned.  Cooperating agencies across Nebraska deployed 350 personnel, while 45 volunteer fire departments from across Nebraska and South Dakota responded to the fire-fighting efforts.

Lightning strikes ignited four wildfires in Keith County that burned grassland and timbers overnight and were contained on the 3rd by noon time. The wildfires occurred at the Eagle Canyon Hideaway that burned up to 3,000 acres of grassland and timber, at the Otter Creek area that burned up to 40,000 acres, at the Ackley Valley on the Hawthorn Ranch that burned up to 6,000, and at the Glen Echo area that burned an estimated 7,500 acres. The Glen Echo wildfire spread into southwest McPherson County before containment.
A lightning strike ignited the McKeage wildfire on the 2nd and was contained by noon time on the 3rd. The fire burned an estimated 7,500 acres of grassland and timber.

A wildfire was ignited by a lightning strike in Keith County at the Glen Echo area that spread into southwest McPherson County overnight. The wildfire burned an estimated 7,500 acres of grassland and timber before containment. Areas of canyon and creek valley were inaccessible for ground firefighting. Rough terrain prevented full containment, but two National Guard UH-60 Black Hawk helicopters provided air support that brought the fire under control before containment.

A wildfire started about one mile north of Interstate 80 near Paxton that was fanned by high winds. The high winds caused the wildfire to quickly spread southeast, crossing Interstate 80 and then burning for an additional 12 miles southeast into northeast Perkins County. The wildfire reached up to 1.5 miles wide. The wildfire destroyed two occupied homes, one abandoned home and various outbuildings were destroyed as well. In addition to building structures the wildfire destroyed several pieces of farm implements, while several power poles and culverts were damaged. The area burned was estimated at 10,000 acres of farm flat and rolling hills. Three firemen developed eye problems with one treated for an unknown illness. The wildfire led to evacuation orders for those in the path of the wildfire from east of Paxton to the south edge of the Keith-Perkins County Line in the southeast.

The Nebraska State Patrol notified WFO North Platte of a plane that took off from the North Platte Regional Airport, Lee Bird Field (LBF) at 1546 CST and lost contact seven minutes later at 1553 CST. At the time weather conditions at LBF included freezing drizzle and visibility of three miles, with a cloud ceiling of 900 feet. The plane was a multi-engine BE-58 manufactured by Raytheon according to a FAA spokeswoman. The plane crashed 11 miles northeast of North Platte in the Maxwell area. Four male fatalities (indirect) occurred in the crash.

A bow echo produced straight-line winds that were estimated up to 80 mph for nearly 30 minutes. The wind damage encompassed over 50 square miles in central and northeast Frontier County, in an area from east of Stockville and west of West Canyon Road to the south and west of Eustis. The high winds produced damage at 12 farmsteads. The most extensive damage just north of County Road 741, where two large metal buildings and nine 10 to 15 thousand bushel silos were destroyed. The wind damage included roofs of homes and outbuildings, windows blown out, over 60 center pivot irrigation systems overturned, large tree limbs down and livestock killed. Flooding occurred along the South Platte River from September 18th through September 26th as water from the historic rains in Colorado moved through the river system. Cropland and pastureland along the river was flooded. Near Big Springs, two businesses sustained minor flood damage, while two truck stops and a motel were closed and evacuated for 48 hours. Road closures included U.S. Highway 138 and Nebraska Link 25B between Interstate 80 and the city of Big Springs. With roads leading into Big Springs being closed, the South Platte Public School was closed on Thursday, September 19th.  Two men were rescued from the river near Big Springs as they were canoeing and capsized. One of the individuals sustained minor injuries.

At least three businesses sustained minor flooding in and near the cities of Brule and Ogallala. Septic problems were noted at several residences around Brule causing some basement damage. Two homes southeast of Roscoe near Nebraska Link 51B suffered severe damage.

Flooding closed South Jeffery Road south of Brady along with the Brady to Moorefield Road and South Banner Road. Other roads were washed out in southeastern Lincoln County. Flooding was a result of the 3 to 5 inches of rain which occurred in southeastern Lincoln County the previous evening.

Minor to moderate flooding began on May 15th along the North Platte River above and below Lake McConaughy.  Flooding was due to excessive runoff in the North Platte River Basin in Wyoming. This coupled with seasonal snow melt, led to high flows along the North Platte River upstream of Lake McConaughy. As the reservoir neared capacity, additional water was released from the lake, resulting in minor to moderate flooding along the North Platte River downstream of Lake McConaughy.  River levels crested at 4.4 feet, 8.9 feet and 6.9 feet at Lisco, Lewellen and North Platte respectively.  The crest was 0.4 feet above the flood stage at Lisco, 1.4 feet above the flood stage at Lewellen and 0.9 feet above the flood stage at North Platte.  One home was evacuated along North River road in North Platte due to the moderate flooding. ||Along the Platte river in eastern Lincoln county, the river reached flood stage on May 23rd and crested on May 31st.  The crest at Brady was 7.8 feet on the 31st, which was 0.3 feet above the flood stage of 7.5 feet.
